title: Ricardo I. Alcalá Briseño, Ph.D.
text:
I am a viral ecologist at Penn State University in the Department of Plant Pathology and Environmental Microbiology (PPEM). My research focuses on the distribution of plant and fungal viromes across natural and agricultural ecosystems, and on understanding their ecological functions alongside the epidemiological dimensions of disease.
I am particularly interested in mixed virus infections and how these interactions shape virome communities and influence pathogen emergence in natural systems. My work centers on developing tools and conceptual frameworks for the analysis of complex interaction-driven datasets, integrating virome network analysis that combines viral metagenomics and meta-transcriptomics with machine-learning approaches and bipartite network analysis.
I synthesize these patterns using concepts from island biogeography, community ecology, and disease ecology to understand how viromes are structured across space, hosts, and ecosystems.


I obtained my Ph.D. from the Plant Pathology Department, the Emerging Pathogen Institute, and the Institute of Food Systems (now the Global Food Systems Institute) at the University of Florida, under the supervision of Professor Karen A. Garrett.
I completed my postdoctoral training in Forest Pathology in the Department of Botany and Plant Pathology at Oregon State University.




I am an Assistant Professor of Viral Ecology at Penn State University in the Department of Plant Pathology and Environmental Microbiology.
My research focuses on plant and fungal viruses across natural and agricultural systems, with an emphasis on virome structure, host–virus interactions, and pathogen emergence.




My doctoral research focused on understanding virome ecological dynamics in crop systems and translating these insights into virome-informed disease management strategies. I am particularly interested in host–virus interactions and virome community assembly, and in identifying the ecological mechanisms that underlie pathogen emergence in complex agroecological landscapes.
My work emphasizes the development of analytical frameworks for complex, interaction-driven datasets. I integrate viral metagenomics and meta-transcriptomics with machine-learning approaches to quantify viral communities, and analyze these data using bipartite network analysis informed by island biogeography and community ecology.

title: Teaching
text:
I taught two courses at Penn State, one 400-level on Viral Ecology (PPEM454), and two modules of the 500-level course of Fundamental of Plant Pathology (PPATH505).
In the Viral Ecology course, I focus on the impact of viruses in natural ecosystems, their roles in major biogeochemical cycles, and their interactions with hosts. The course combines full lectures covering foundational knowledge of viruses—from taxonomy to virome analysis—with applied topics such as outbreaks, spillover events, zoonoses, and epidemics. I provide students with exposure to quantitative and disease ecology through applied bioinformatics workflows, including genome assembly and BLAST-based analyses.
In Fundamentals of Plant Pathology, I cover pathogen biology, lifestyles, systematics, and evolution. In the first module, I provide a detailed introduction to the diverse lifestyles of plant pathogens, the traits that define pathogenicity, and the molecular arsenals—such as effector repertoires and genomic indicators—associated with host infection. In the second module, I focus on hands-on analyses of genome-based phylogenetics and evolutionary relationships among plant pathogens.
I mentor a couple of grad students, and undergrad students in virology and bioinformatics.

title: PUBLICATION
Research
text:
I am developing a network framework for the analysis of complex viromes in the agroecological landscape, by applying concepts of island biogeography, network analysis and metagenomics. The bipartite network structure explains very intuitively the association of virus and plant–hosts, describing ecological patterns of interactions such as nested and modular. Understanding community structure of viruses, we can translate that knowledge into management strategies and apply other plant disease ecology. A long-term goal of this work is to create a more quantitative approach for understanding community assembly rules and for predicting future emerging pathogens.
Virome dynamics respond to the distribution of plants, changes in the landscape for agricultural usage and climate change alter the patterns of distribution of hosts, and vectors, therefore the landscape connectivity allow emerging pathogens to establish in new niches. We are comparing host and location combinations to determine ecological patterns, viral positive and negative interactions, and spatial relationships.

title: Research
text:
Diversity of viruses: Viral discovery
Viral metagenomics is a useful tool for assessing the diversity of viruses. Using high-throughput sequencing (HTS) has become the standard tool for virus diagnosis, and the to go tool for revealing associations of viruses within the plant host. Viruses interactions occur at different levels within plant-host, causing necrosis, mosaics, stunting symptoms and some times, asymptomatic. Another interesting feature is that this technique reveals multiple interactions that otherwise would have been difficult to identify, in most cases when an unknown virus is present within the same plant.
